message:
feat(update): a payload name is data, not a path

Names arrive in a manifest and get joined to the install directory by something
running as administrator. Used as given, that is a primitive for writing
anywhere on the machine.

The signature is the first lock and this is the second. Defence in depth means
not relying on the signature having been checked correctly, on the signing key
never leaking, or on the publishing side never being talked into signing
something odd -- none of those failures should end in a write outside the
install directory.

Names are refused, never sanitised. Deciding whether a name is already safe is
a far smaller problem than making an unsafe one safe, and the set the product
actually ships is small and boring.

Three Windows-specific traps get particular attention. NUL, CON and COM1 do not
name files at all -- a payload called NUL would make a swap appear to succeed
while writing nothing -- so they are matched exactly, on the stem, without
catching NULL.txt or COM10. Windows silently strips a trailing dot or space, so
"a." and "a" are one file and two entries could collide without looking like
duplicates. And a colon after the first character is an alternate data stream,
which writes hidden content into a file that already exists.

Both separator forms are checked, because a name can look harmless in one and
hostile in the other. That caught a bug in this code: splitting on backslash
alone read "ui/.." as a single component and rejected it for ending in a dot --
still a refusal, but the wrong reason, which hides a real traversal behind a
cosmetic complaint.

Duplicates are refused for a concrete reason rather than tidiness. The swap
moves every named file aside before writing any of them, so the same name twice
would have the second move-aside overwrite the first file's backup, and a
rollback would restore the wrong bytes. Case and separator differences count as
the same name, because the filesystem thinks so.

Wired into the config's validate(), which AcquireLock calls first -- so one bad
name means the update never starts.

qwinsta: console active, rdp-tcp listening. 54 checks here, 498 across the
eight update suites. The three live PIDs are unchanged.
